One simple distinction: traditional construction builds on site, while prefabricated installation assembles on site what a factory has already produced. Assembly speed and connection quality determine the value of this trade.

It does not suit people who fear heights, avoid sun exposure, or cannot tolerate dust. The work takes place outdoors and inside unfinished structures, with summer heat and winter cold as routine conditions.

A common path starts as a general construction laborer or assembly worker, continues through crew-based training in lifting and connection methods, adds credentials such as construction electrician or welder certificates, and leads to independent installation-team leadership. People with carpentry, plumbing, or electrical backgrounds transition faster.
This work suits physically fit, agile people who can understand simple drawings. Construction experience and familiarity with electric drills and pneumatic nailers support a quick start.

Manufactured Building and Mobile Home Installers assemble factory-produced building modules, wall panels, and roof sections into finished structures on site. Their work includes lifted placement, structural connections, plumbing, electrical and gas hookups, and interior and exterior finishing.

paragraphs: The day's pace follows lifting windows. At the morning briefing, verify deliveries and the lifting plan. Once the crane is positioned, match each wall panel to its designated location, tighten bolts, and fully apply sealant. Complete plumbing and electrical hookups and finish details in the afternoon. Before leaving, count tools and inspect edge protection. A single-family home often rises from nothing within two or three days.

In short, they bring factory-produced wall panels and building sections to a site, lift them into position, connect them into one structure, and hook up utilities. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data show about 3,100 manufactured-building and mobile-home installers employed in 2024, projected to rise to 3,300 by 2034. That is a net increase of about 200 jobs, with roughly 300 annual openings. Median annual pay is about $41,100 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace manufactured-building installers, but it will transform the first half of installation. BIM models can generate installation sequences directly, QR scans verify components, and lifting-plan software runs simulations. These tools end the era of guessing locations from drawings. Yet job sites have no perfect template. Crane angles, wind loads, component damage, and deviations from site construction all require installers to make immediate judgments that AI cannot handle soon.
